docs.title: TIDE — Time Invariant Discretization Engine
docs.text:
TIDE bins features for credit scorecards so that the bins are stable over time. In every period of the training data, as hard constraints:

  • the event rate is monotonic over the bins, in the same direction in all periods, so WoE / event-rate curves of different bins never cross;
  • adjacent bins differ in event rate by at least min_er_delta;
  • every bin holds at least min_sample_rate of the period's rows and at least min_class_obs events and non-events.

It works on mixed-type columns, e.g. age = [18, 44, np.nan, "special_category", -999], and encodes them with Weight of Evidence. It is a scikit-learn transformer.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pip install tide-binning

Requires Python ≥ 3.10. All dependencies (numpy, pandas, scipy, scikit-learn, matplotlib, joblib, tqdm) ship prebuilt wheels for Windows, macOS and Linux.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
from tide import TIDE

X = pd.DataFrame(...)          # features, may be mixed-type
y = pd.Series(...)             # binary target, 0/1
periods = pd.Series(...)       # e.g. application month: str, datetime, Period, int, ...

binner = TIDE(cat_values=[-999])          # -999 is a category, not a number
X_woe = binner.fit_transform(X, y, periods=periods)

lr = LogisticRegression().fit(X_woe, y)
print(roc_auc_score(y, lr.predict_proba(X_woe)[:, 1]))

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
binner.summary_       # one row per feature: trend, n_bins, IV, max PSI, warnings
binner.stats_         # per feature and bin: n_obs, event rate, WoE, IV
binner.stats_per_     # per period, feature and bin: n_obs, event rate, PSI
binner.bins_          # fitted bins (format below)
binner.woes_          # {feature: {bin_idx: WoE}}
binner.plot(["age"])  # bin sizes and event rates, event rate over time, PSI over time

docs.title: Bins format
docs.text:
{"trend": "pos",
 "bins": {0: {(-np.inf, 25.0): "cont", "special_category": "cat"},
          1: {(25.0, 40.0): "cont"},
          2: {(40.0, np.inf): "cont"},
          3: {None: "missing"}}}       # None = NaN / None / pd.NA / NaT

Intervals are (a, b] for a positive trend and [a, b) for a negative trend, so a value that is unseen in training and lies between two borders always goes to the bin with the higher event rate.

docs.title: Handling special values
docs.text:
You have Use NaN, None, pd.NA, NaT missing automatically strings, bools categories automatically numeric codes such as -999 that mean "no data" missing_values=[-999] numeric codes that are a category of their own cat_values=[-999] different codes per feature {"age": [-1], "income": [-999]}

missing_strategy ("separate_bin", "worst_bin", "best_bin") and cat_strategy ("separate_bin", "chi-squared", "tide") control how they are binned. With cat_strategy="tide", all bins — continuous, categorical and missing — are merged until the stability constraints hold for all of them.

docs.title: Your own bins
docs.text:
binner = TIDE(user_bins={"age": {"trend": "pos", "bins": {
    0: {(-np.inf, 25.0): "cont"},
    1: {(25.0, 60.0): "cont"},
    2: {(60.0, np.inf): "cont", None: "missing"},
}}})

User bins are applied as given (U-shapes are fine); a warning lists training values that fall in no bin.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
import pickle
binner = pickle.load(open("binner.pkl", "rb"))
binner.set_params(handle_unknown="worst")   # change how unseen values are treated, no refit
X_woe = binner.transform(X_new)

handle_unknown: "keep" (leave the raw value), "worst" / "best" (lowest / highest WoE), "missing_worst" / "missing_best" (WoE of the missing bin, else lowest / highest).

docs.title: scikit-learn
docs.text:
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_validate

pipe = Pipeline([("tide", TIDE()), ("lr", LogisticRegression())])
pipe.fit(X, y, tide__periods=periods)
cross_validate(pipe, X, y, params={"tide__periods": periods}, scoring="roc_auc")

get_params / set_params / clone, get_feature_names_out and metadata routing (TIDE().set_fit_request(periods=True)) work as usual.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
fit works on per-period counts of the sorted unique values, so after one sort per feature its cost no longer depends on the number of rows. n_jobs=-1 fits features in parallel. Measured on a 2-core laptop, 5,000,000 rows and 24 periods, per feature:

feature fit transform integer, 100 unique values ~1 s ~0.5 s float, 1,000 unique ~1 s ~0.5 s float, all unique (undersampled to 200 quantiles) ~5 s ~0.5 s float, 530k unique (exact search, max_unique=10**6) ~5 s ~0.5 s mixed object column (numbers, strings, NaN) ~3 s ~2 s

Run python benchmarks/bench_fit.py to measure on your machine.

docs.title: Algorithm
docs.text:
For each feature:

  1. Split the column into continuous values (real numbers), categories (strings, bools, cat_values) and missing values (NaN-likes, missing_values).
  2. Trend. Unless forced, the sign of the slope of a linear fit of event rate against the index of max(3, ceil(ln n)) quantile bins of the continuous part.
  3. Candidate axis. The sorted unique continuous values — or n_quantiles quantiles when there are more than max_unique of them. With missing_strategy="worst_bin" / "best_bin" and a missing share below missing_rate, the missing values are placed at the worst / best end of the axis.
  4. Greedy scan. From the start of the axis, the bin [base..k] is a valid candidate if, in every period:
    • its cumulative event rate equals the minimum (positive trend) / maximum (negative trend) over all its extensions [base..j], j ≥ k — so the next bin can only have a higher (lower) rate;
    • it holds ≥ min_sample_rate of the period's rows and ≥ min_class_obs events and non-events;
    • its rate differs from the previous bin's by ≥ min_er_delta;
    • and the split lies between two continuous points.

The first valid k is taken if the remainder can still form a valid bin; otherwise the scan stops and the remainder is the last bin. If the last bin breaks min_er_delta, it is merged into its neighbour. 5. Categories. Separate bins, ChiMerge (Kerber, 1992), or the TIDE merge: until no two bins' event-rate curves cross and every constraint holds, the worst bin is merged with the closest one (squared event-rate distance); continuous bins only merge with adjacent ones. 6. WoE / IV / PSI: WoE = ln((%nonevents + ε) / (%events + ε)), IV = Σ (%nonevents − %events) · WoE, PSI = Σ (%new − %old) · ln(%new / (%old + ε)), ε = 1e-8.

Exact search on many unique values

A candidate must be the lowest (highest) cumulative event rate from that point on in every period simultaneously. With hundreds of thousands of candidate points, each step adds only a few rows, the rate jitters, and with many periods such a point may never exist — the feature then becomes a single bin. Lowering max_unique makes the scan work on quantiles instead, which smooths the jitter.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
Bases: TransformerMixin, BaseEstimator

TIDE - Time Invariant Discretization Engine.

Bins mixed-type features (numbers, strings, missing values) so that the bins are stable over time, and encodes them with Weight of Evidence. For the continuous part the following hard constraints hold in every period:

  • the event rate is monotonic over the bins, in the same direction in all periods, so event-rate (WoE) curves never cross;
  • adjacent bins differ in event rate by at least min_er_delta;
  • every bin holds at least min_sample_rate of the period's rows and at least min_class_obs events and non-events.

By default, categories and missing values get their own bins. With cat_strategy="tide", all bins (continuous, categorical and missing) are merged until the constraints hold for all of them.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default min_sample_rate float

Minimum share of a period's rows in each bin, checked in every period.

0.05 min_class_obs int

Minimum number of events and of non-events in each bin, in every period.

1 min_er_delta float

Minimum event-rate gap between adjacent continuous bins, in every period.

0.0 trend ('auto', 'pos', 'neg')

Direction of the event rate over the continuous bins. "auto" uses the sign of a linear fit of event rate vs. quantile-bin index. A dict maps feature names to "pos" / "neg" / "auto"; features that are not listed use "auto".

"auto" max_unique int

If the continuous part has more unique values than this, the candidate split points are n_quantiles quantiles instead of all unique values.

1000 n_quantiles int

Number of quantile candidate points used when max_unique is exceeded.

200 n_trend_bins 'log' or int

Number of quantile bins for trend detection. "log" means max(3, ceil(ln(n_rows))).

"log" min_bound float or 'col_min' / 'col_max'

Outer bounds of the first and last continuous bins. "col_min" / "col_max" use the training minimum / maximum, so unseen values beyond them are unknown.

-inf / inf max_bound float or 'col_min' / 'col_max'

Outer bounds of the first and last continuous bins. "col_min" / "col_max" use the training minimum / maximum, so unseen values beyond them are unknown.

-inf / inf missing_values list or dict

Extra values treated as missing, e.g. [-1, "N/A"]. NaN, None, pd.NA and NaT are always missing. A dict maps feature names to lists.

() cat_values list or dict

Numeric values treated as categories, e.g. [-999]. Strings and bools are always categories. A dict maps feature names to lists.

() missing_strategy ('separate_bin', 'worst_bin', 'best_bin')

"separate_bin": missing values get their own bin (if any are present). "worst_bin" / "best_bin": if the missing share is below missing_rate, missing values join the continuous bin with the highest / lowest event rate and take part in the scan; otherwise they get their own bin.

"separate_bin" missing_rate float

Threshold for "worst_bin" / "best_bin".

0.05 cat_strategy ('separate_bin', 'chi-squared', 'tide')

"separate_bin": every category is its own bin; curves may cross. "chi-squared": categories are merged with ChiMerge. "tide": all bins are merged until every constraint holds for all bins.

"separate_bin" alpha_significance float

p-value threshold for ChiMerge.

0.05 user_bins dict or None

{feature: bins_dict}. These features are not searched; their bins are applied as given. A warning lists training values that fall in no bin.

None handle_unknown ('keep', 'worst', 'best', 'missing_worst', 'missing_best')

How transform treats values that fall in no bin. "keep" leaves the raw value, "worst" / "best" use the lowest / highest WoE, and "missing_worst" / "missing_best" use the WoE of the bin with missing values, else the lowest / highest WoE. It is read only in transform, so it can be changed with set_params after fitting.

"keep" n_jobs int or None

Number of parallel jobs over features (joblib). -1 uses all cores.

None verbose bool

Show a progress bar during fit.

False

Attributes:

Name Type Description bins_ dict

{feature: bins_dict}.

woes_ dict

{feature: {bin_idx: WoE}}.

stats_ DataFrame

Per feature and bin: counts, event rate, WoE and IV.

stats_per_ DataFrame

Per period, feature and bin: counts, event rate and PSI.

summary_ DataFrame

One row per feature: trend, number of bins, IV, max PSI and warnings.

periods_ Index

Sorted unique periods seen in fit.

feature_names_in_ ndarray

Feature names seen in fit.

n_features_in_ int

Number of features seen in fit.

Complete rewrite. The greedy algorithm and its rules are unchanged: on the scenarios in tests/golden, the bins are identical to v0.5.0.

docs.title: New
docs.text:
• scikit-learn estimator: get_params / set_params / clone, Pipeline, cross_validate(params={"tide__periods": ...}), metadata routing, get_feature_names_out.
  • NaN / None / pd.NA / NaT are supported in features (bins key None).
  • cat_values and missing_values turn numeric codes such as -999 into categories or missing values, globally or per feature.
  • trend can be forced ("pos" / "neg"), globally or per feature.
  • max_unique / n_quantiles (defaults 1000 / 200): features with more than 1000 unique values are split at 200 quantiles instead of every unique value. This is faster, and with many periods the exact search often finds no split at all. Pass a large max_unique for v0.5 behaviour.
  • user_bins: apply your own bins (any shape), with a coverage warning.
  • summary_ table; a warning when a feature collapses to one continuous bin.
  • n_jobs (parallel over features) and verbose (progress bar).
  • plot() returns the figures and accepts show=False.
  • Periods may be any sortable type and need not be sorted.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• min_er_delta is now also guaranteed for the last bin (it is merged otherwise).
  • min_er_delta no longer applies to the first bin (v0.5 required its event rate ≥ delta).
  • With worst_bin / best_bin, no split is made between the continuous part and the attached missing values.
  • cat_strategy="tide" now guarantees all constraints: continuous bins merge only with adjacent ones (their intervals become one), and their monotonicity is re-checked. The missing bin takes part in the merge.
  • transform no longer mistakes values equal to a WoE for unknown values.
  • stats_per no longer duplicates rows on refit.
  • "col_min" / "col_max" bounds now use the next representable float instead of ± 1e-8, which failed for large values.

docs.title: Changed (breaking)
docs.text:
• WoE uses a symmetric epsilon, ln((%nonevents + 1e-8) / (%events + 1e-8)): a bin without non-events no longer gets WoE = -inf and IV = inf. Other bins are unchanged up to ~1e-8.
  • fit(X, y, per) → fit(X, y, periods); reset and return_bins were removed.
  • handle_unknown moved from transform() into the constructor (set_params changes it).
  • transform requires the same columns as fit; xnames and ndarray input were removed.
  • Attributes: exog_bins → bins_, exog_woes → woes_, stats → stats_, stats_per → stats_per_; the stats tables have a new bin_idx column.
  • missing_categories → missing_values; n_prebins → n_trend_bins.
  • Bin labels (stats tables and plots) show integer bounds without decimals ((18,25]) and other bounds with exactly 4 decimals ((0.3400,1.1130]). bins_ keeps the full values.

docs.title: Choosing periods
docs.text: TIDE checks every constraint in every period, so the periods define what "stable" means. Pick the granularity that matches how the model will be monitored (month, quarter, ...), and drop broken or irrelevant periods before calling fit. More periods mean stricter binning: with many small periods, noisy features may collapse to one bin (you get a warning and summary_.n_cont_bins == 1).

docs.title: Reading the results
docs.text:
• summary_ — start here: IV, number of bins, maximum PSI and warnings per feature.
  • stats_ — the classic binning table for the whole sample.
  • stats_per_ — the same per period, with PSI against the previous (PSI_seq) and the first (PSI_base) period.
  • plot() — three panels per feature for reports: bin sizes and event rates, event rate of each bin over time, and bin shares with PSI over time.

docs.title: Parameters that matter most
docs.text: Parameter Effect min_sample_rate Larger → fewer, larger bins. Checked per period. min_class_obs Larger → no bins with very few events in some period. min_er_delta Larger → adjacent bins must be clearly different in every period. max_unique, n_quantiles When a feature has more than max_unique (default 1000) unique values, only n_quantiles (default 200) quantiles are candidate split points. Integer features such as age keep their exact search. trend Force "pos" / "neg" when business logic dictates the direction. missing_strategy Separate bin for missing values, or join them to the worst / best bin when they are rare. cat_strategy Keep categories separate, ChiMerge them, or merge everything for full stability ("tide").

docs.title: Manual binning
docs.text:
Fit once, inspect bins_, edit the dict and pass it back as user_bins — any shape is allowed, including U-shapes. The "trend" key selects the bracket convention: (a, b] for "pos", [a, b) for "neg".

binner = TIDE().fit(X, y, periods)
bins = binner.bins_["age"]
bins["bins"][0] = {(-np.inf, 30.0): "cont"}   # edit
binner2 = TIDE(user_bins={"age": bins}).fit(X, y, periods)
